The drag reduction "upgrade" turns the game into an uncontrollable nightmare. Other issues that make the game "not fun" for me include * Zero account progression. Your first game is exactly like your fiftieth. * No saves or checkpoints. * No real guides and no one seems to know the rules of the game. * The game is only a couple hours long, but with frequent instant deaths (and my first game I just died without seeing whatever killed me at all) to pad play time. * Forums seem to lack concrete information and the fans are pretty toxic to people who have issues with the game. (git gud doesn't help when I died to nothing I could see) * Controls feel incredibly clunky and awkward.

tldr: It's just too expensive for what it is right now. Could be great when finished. You're probably here because you saw this on YouTube and got hyped for this re-imagining of the cell phase of Spore. So was I. In fact, I was so hyped I bought this for 17 euro's. Now I kind of regret that. The core mechanic looks great in principle, and is actually versatile, but almost never viable as a means of beating the game. There are explosives, lightning, acid, poison, lasers and spikes to use as weapons, the first 4 of which require such a specific mix of secondary cells that they will inevitably either kill you or get you killed for not having a complete build. And even if you do manage to find them, the build feels weak, fragile and likely to damage yourself. Lasers can only be found in higher levels (I think) can overheat and are also weak, and that leaves spikes as the only viable build. Which is kind of a let down. I've build homing explosives, a spinning acid sprayer, lightning rods, and they were all functional, but non of them really worked. And most ended up killing me as well as some weak enemies. Another annoyance is the game withholds information. It has descriptions of drag, overheating, voltages, or regeneration, and many more but it doesn't tell you when this'll happen, or how much it is impacted by cells. You just start dying, or you just can't turn anymore. And you'll die so fast trial and error isn't really an option. Lastly, the controls don't feel nice. It's almost like a cheap way to make the game a bit harder. And no controller support as of now. This has potential. Lots. But it needs work to be fun as a game. Also lots.

There's no real reason why this game should be a rouge-lite and not just a sandbox or have checkpoints at each "level" death can come very suddenly which never feels good especially here when death literally just means you wasted the time entirely. Like sure. You now know a unique build and maybe you saved it, cool. But you will still need to find all of the parts you had before or at least try and find another unique build. Which there are many but, finding new "cells" is quite annoying and not exactly streamlined. You really do need to just swim around looking for them. Either way, would i recommend this game to someone? Hell no. Not at the price its at.

Life... Life finds a way... to murder all other life it sees. [h1]Dawkins can suck a big fat one[/h1] Random evolution? Not here, baby! This is intelligent design! Well, maybe not all that intelligent, given how it's you and me doing this while thing. But malicious? Definitely. OK, so what you do in this game is design a little critter with only one goal: To kill every other critter it encounters. The more the better. The ocean is a more beautiful place when it's empty. You do this by slapping together different kinds of cells into something that sort of resembles a primitive, jawless fish. No kidding. You want jaws? You gotta find the right cells and assemble them yourself into a decent set of chompers. And between you and me, chomper builds aren't peak. Fun. But not peak. But that's basically this entire game: You assemble some kind of hellish fish creature out of the different types of cells you collect. What makes the game shine is that the different kinds of cells work great together in all kinds of nefarious combinations. Want to shoot homing missiles like you're a barely multicellurar Top Gun? You can do that. Want to spin around as an electrified disco ball of death in perpetual risk of burning out but shedding your outer layer to prevent that? You can do that. Want to shoot streams of acid and make them achieve some real distance by pairing them with water jets? You can do that. It'll make your PC chug harder than a 28 year old frat guy trying to stave off impending responsibility, but you can do that. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] A much more degenerate man than me once described the ocean as "perpetual vore hell", and utlimately that's what this entire game is about. Have a plan to eat every being you ever meet. Grow big. Hueg, even. And despite technically not having one, use your brain. Only smart designs actually win. Because yeah, this game's kinda hard. But it's the sort of hard that makes it tick. Or throb. OK, that's my cue to end this review. Good game, seems expensive but is lowkey worth it. Nothing else does this particular genre quite this well.

Deceptively fun little freakbuilder where you collect pixel-like cells and build contraption-like critters. It's got some early access jank and the UI is a little wonky but this really stimulates my creativity.

I love the concept of building a character from the cell up. However, the gameplay doesn't really pan out. It's very frustrating trial and error with little in the way of personal reward, at least for me. I feel other games have done the overall gameplay concept better (start small, eat other things, get bigger and badder) because they were more accessible. You would really have to love min/maxing or the core conceit of this game... which I think makes it pretty niche. Not a fan at all. I would have asked for a refund, but I considered it a donation to a dev who clearly had a passion for a very high-functioning concept that just... doesn't pan out. Not for myself, at least.

This is spore cell stage: indie dev edition. IMO, wait on this one. It's interesting but it needs to cook a bit more and the asking price is high for a little EA game. Pain points for me: * The UI isn't easy to use, especially the cell select creature builder that leaves all your parts randomly scattered around the build area and wiggling around. I spent way too much time trying to find where that one cell slid off to. * No save points whatsoever. You're either playing sandbox or doing an 'ironman' run. * Not a lot of explaining of what does what (but then it's still Early Access). * The dark caves are a paaian to enter when you don't have a light to navigate them with, and the part doesn't always spawn in somewhere accessible. * The genome stat is annoyingly restrictive * The electrical/logic system isn't very easy to use when you start wanting something more than simple circuits. A diode cell would go a long way here. Still, an interesting way to kill your free time.

Primordialis presents you with a solid and engaging customization system in which the player is free to construct any sort of monstrous organism they can imagine from a variety of unique little cell parts. Through experimentation and clever combination, a lot of impressive things can be made. There is even plenty of room for artistic expression with the ability to change the color of each individual cell. It's a system that has a lot of promise, and at first glance it seems like it can carry with it a lot of fun. Unfortunately, this system is surrounded by and beaten down by the core gameplay mechanics of the Rogue-like genre... In the standard mode you start with essentially nothing. A few generic cell pieces and pocket change worth of points to spend making your organism, which of course is fine. There has to be some sort of progression. Though it's all locked solely behind the RNG aspects of procedurally generated rogue-like world wherein the player will find themself spending a not insignificant amount of time and effort just to create something that's not only effective but also something they personally enjoy. Iteration by iteration, finding cell parts, experimenting with them, and leveling up so they can afford to construct what they like. It's all pretty par-for-the-course in terms of Rogue-like progression, but that's exactly the issue. All that effort and time spent finding parts, experimenting with them, building your organism, and even giving it a paint job can vanish in an instant to any of several various gimmick enemies, such as jet propelled jaws that may pin you to a wall or even an actual rail gun that can eviscerate you in as little as a singular well placed shot. Then it's just gone. There is no meta progression to compensate the lose of all that effort. This is a Rogue-LIKE, not a Rogue-LITE. One life. If you die you lose it all. So all that effort you put into creating your unique, one of a kind, specifically to your tastes creature? Gone. Except for perhaps the design you saved of it, though in the grand scheme of things that's not really going to help much in the face of standard Rogue-like RNG because you'll to grind through the whole process once again to level back up and find each cell once again to recreate that thing you liked. Or, alternatively, you could cave in and just make a ball with spikes to get through the game, of which there isn't even much of with there being.. only 5 primary biomes and a few secondary. All of which are pretty barren, only offering some change of hue to visually distinguish it from the previous and some new things to try and kill you. It all begins to feel very samey quite quickly, and even the perks you get from defeating the bosses are few in variety and meager in power. Overall, the game's core mechanic clashes violently with the nature of it's genre. It's too much effort to collect the desired cells to build something you like only to lose everything to what will most likely be something entirely absurd. It has potential. It can even be fun for a while. Though in it's current state the gameplay loop is arduous, the world is dull, and I don't believe there is enough content to warrant the $20 USD price tag.

It's pretty fun, and it's EA so I'm going to give it a little grace here and give a thumbs up. The game drops you into the first area. You have two cells to choose from to get started. You kill a single weak enemy, immediately go to level 5, and then there's a bunch more cells waiting outside the start area. You explore the first area crushing the creatures, leveling up, and finally killing this weird fish that turns out to be the area boss and you get to select a mutation. First area done, ez pz, but it takes a bit of time swimming around and exploring to collect stuff. Then you go into the rapids and head to the 2nd area, and you get killed in a single attack. You do the first part again, get built up, and go back and get killed in a single attack again by something different. You repeat this until you can figure out how to not die in the second area. It's like dying to a boss in Dark Souls and having a long run back each time. I'm still trying to get past that. Outside of the area difficulty, the gameplay loop doesn't flow super well imo. You'll spend a ton of time adjusting your body as you level up and get room for more cells. You play a little bit, level up, and then spend time adjusting your body and figuring things out. You then play just a little bit more, level up more, and do that same thing again. Honestly time spent for me was around 80% of time adjusting my body with 20% of the time actually playing. -------------------------- It's not great, but it's not bad. I'm charmed by the ideas present, but put off by the execution. Hopefully with more time in the oven it gets better.

This is a somewhat refreshing take on the typical "ship builder" game. "Somewhat refreshing" because it lacks polish and gameplay smoothing it will likely have in full release. Overall, it has basic RNG, interesting AI on enemies so you can't just cheese everything, interactive build combos, and a clear open ended structure to really play with the mechanics of the game. Pros: fun to play around with builds, core mechanics are solid, each run has enough difference to keep it fresh. Cons: too little info to really dive into builds without extensive testing, there is a clear "meta" where certain builds will just get you nuked, not enough info on how you died (most deaths were met with a "how did I die???")
